description: Nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex families. The Rapoports on five types of family diversity.
content_html:
What Is a Family?

There is no single, universally agreed definition of a family in sociology. Rather than adopting one definition as correct, sociologists study the variety of household and kinship arrangements that people live in and the social meanings attached to them. The UK is home to a range of family diversity — different family forms that have become increasingly common since the mid-twentieth century. Understanding each form factually, without privileging one as “normal”, is a key sociological skill.

Major Family Forms in the UK

The following family forms are identified and studied by sociologists:

  • Nuclear family: two parents and their dependent children living together as a self-contained unit. Functionalists such as Parsons argued this is the most efficient family form for modern industrial society.
  • Extended family: a family network that extends beyond the nuclear unit to include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Extended families may be vertically extended (three or more generations) or horizontally extended (relatives of the same generation).
  • Reconstituted family: also called a blended family, formed when two adults — at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship — form a new household together. Reconstituted families have grown in number as divorce rates have risen and remarriage or repartnering has become more common.
  • Lone parent family: one parent living with and responsible for dependent children. ONS data shows that around one in four families with dependent children in the UK is a lone parent family. The majority of lone parents are women.
  • Single sex (same-sex) family: a family in which both parents are of the same sex, including same-sex couples raising children. The Civil Partnership Act 2004 and Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 gave same-sex couples in the UK formal legal recognition.
  • Cohabiting family: a couple (same-sex or different-sex) living together without being married or in a civil partnership, who may or may not have children. Cohabitation has grown significantly in the UK since the 1970s.
Key Fact

The AQA specification identifies five family forms: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex. Each describes a different household arrangement. Sociologists study all of them as legitimate family forms without privileging one as the correct or normal version.

Global Family Forms

The spec notes that family forms differ not only within the UK but within a global context. Key examples include:

  • Kibbutz: a collective settlement in which property and sometimes child rearing are shared among the community as a whole. The kibbutz challenged the assumption that child rearing is always a private family function.
  • Polygamy: marriage to more than one spouse simultaneously. Polygyny (one man, multiple wives) is practised in some societies; polyandry (one woman, multiple husbands) is rare. Both are illegal in the UK.

The Rapoports: Five Types of Family Diversity

Rhona and Robert Rapoport argued that British society is characterised by diversity rather than a single dominant family form. Rather than simply counting different family structures, they identified five distinct dimensions of family diversity in their 1982 analysis:

  • Organisational diversity: differences in the way families divide paid and unpaid work. For example, dual-career families versus families with a traditional breadwinner-homemaker split.
  • Cultural diversity: differences related to ethnicity and religion. For example, South Asian families in the UK may have stronger extended kinship networks than White British families; Muslim, Hindu or Jewish families may organise family life differently in relation to gender roles and marriage practices.
  • Social class diversity: working-class and middle-class families differ in income, housing, parenting styles and the opportunities available to children.
  • Life cycle diversity: family structure changes across an individual’s life — a young childless couple, a family with young children, an empty nest family and a widowed individual are all at different life cycle stages.
  • Cohort diversity: people born in different generations have experienced different historical conditions — attitudes to divorce, cohabitation and same-sex partnerships differ markedly between older and younger cohorts.

Not all sociologists regard the growth of family diversity as equally welcome. The New Right, associated with sociologists such as Charles Murray, views the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation with concern, arguing that the breakdown of the traditional nuclear family is linked to a range of social problems including poverty, crime and educational underachievement. Murray argued that lone parent households contribute to a dependency culture and an “underclass”.

Feminist sociologists, by contrast, tend to view the growth of family diversity as reflecting women’s greater economic independence and freedom to leave unhappy marriages and partnerships. From a feminist perspective, the decline of the traditional nuclear family represents progress rather than crisis. Postmodernist sociologists argue that diversity and individual choice are defining features of contemporary life and that no single family form can be presented as superior to others.

Key Fact

The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort. These show that the family is not a single fixed institution but varies across time, culture and circumstance.

Students sometimes write that “the nuclear family is dying out.” This is an overstatement. ONS data consistently shows that the nuclear family (married or cohabiting couple with dependent children) remains the most common family form in the UK. What has changed is that other family forms have grown in proportion — particularly lone parent families and cohabiting couples. The sociological point is not that the nuclear family has disappeared but that it is no longer the only family form encountered by the majority of the population. The Rapoports’ five types of diversity capture the complexity better than a simple “nuclear family is declining” claim.
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question about family forms, identify the specific family form clearly (1 mark) and then develop your description with at least two additional points (2 marks). For example: “A reconstituted family is formed when two adults, at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship, form a new household. It is also called a blended family and has become more common as divorce rates have risen.” This answer identifies (reconstituted), describes the defining feature (one or both adults has children from a previous relationship), adds a synonym and links to a social trend — earning all three marks. A common mistake is identifying the family form in one sentence and stopping there, earning only 1 mark. On a 12-mark Discuss about family diversity, never assert that one family form is better or worse than another — present the New Right, feminist and postmodernist views as competing perspectives and let your conclusion weigh the evidence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The AQA specification identifies five family forms: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex. The UK also contains cohabiting families, and global examples include the kibbutz and polygamous family forms.
  • The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort — showing that family diversity runs deeper than simply counting different household structures.
  • Perspectives on family diversity differ: New Right sociologists (Murray) view the growth of lone parent families with concern; feminist sociologists see it as reflecting women's greater independence; postmodernist sociologists celebrate diversity and individual choice as defining features of contemporary life.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a reconstituted family?
A) Two parents and their biological children living together
B) Grandparents, parents and children living in the same household
C) A family formed when two adults, at least one with children from a previous relationship, form a new household
D) A single parent living with dependent children
practice_questions.marks: C) A family formed when two adults, at least one with children from a previous relationship, form a new household [1 mark]

1 mark for indicating that it refers to a variety of family structures or household arrangements; 1 mark for indicating that these exist within a society (rather than a single dominant form). Example: 'Family diversity refers to the variety of different family structures and household arrangements found within a society, rather than a single dominant family form.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of the Rapoports' five types of family diversity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming one of the five types (organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle, cohort). 2 marks for a developed description with an example: e.g. 'Cultural diversity refers to differences in family organisation related to ethnicity and religion — for example, some South Asian families in the UK maintain stronger extended kinship networks than White British families, while different religious traditions shape marriage and gender role practices differently.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the New Right view of increasing family diversity in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the New Right as a perspective that views family diversity with concern. 1 mark for naming Murray or referencing the New Right's concern about lone parent families. 1 mark for explaining the argument: the breakdown of the traditional nuclear family is linked to social problems (poverty, crime, educational underachievement). 1 mark for a further development: e.g. Murray's underclass thesis argues that lone parent households contribute to a dependency culture where welfare dependency is passed between generations.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe two different family forms found in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Name two distinct family forms (e.g. lone parent family and extended family) for 1 mark each identification. 1 mark for a developed description of either one that includes a defining feature or relevant detail: e.g. 'A lone parent family consists of one parent living with and responsible for dependent children without a resident partner. ONS data shows around one in four families with dependent children in the UK is a lone parent family, with the majority of lone parents being women.'

practice_questions.text: "Family diversity in the UK is a positive development for society." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained, two-sided argument covering at least two contrasting perspectives. Arguments in favour: feminist view that diversity reflects women's greater economic independence and freedom from constraining relationships; postmodernist view that diversity and individual choice are defining features of contemporary life; the Rapoports' research showing that diversity is multi-dimensional (not just structural but cultural, class-based and generational), suggesting no single family form meets everyone's needs equally. Arguments against: New Right perspective (Murray) that the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation undermines social stability, leads to poverty and educational underachievement, and fosters a dependency culture. Functionalist perspective that the nuclear family is the most efficient unit for primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately (family diversity, patriarchy, underclass, reconstituted, cohort diversity). A supported judgement that weighs the evidence.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present, named sociologists referenced, judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing (4–6 marks): Mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description. Few named sociologists. Little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologists identified five types of family diversity in Britain in 1982?
A family consisting of one parent and their dependent children, without a resident partner, is called a _____ family.
The Rapoports' type of family diversity that refers to differences related to ethnicity and religion is called _____ diversity.
A family formed when two adults, at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship, form a new household is called a _____ or blended family.
Match each Rapoport diversity type to its description:
right: Differences in how families divide paid and unpaid work between partners
Family structure changes as individuals move through different life stages
People born in different generations have experienced different historical conditions and hold different attitudes

glossary_terms.definition: The variety of different family structures and household arrangements found within a society, rather than a single dominant family form.
A family unit consisting of two parents and their dependent children, living together as a self-contained unit.
A family network that extends beyond the nuclear unit to include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins.
A family formed when two adults, at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship, form a new household together; also called a blended family.
A family consisting of one parent living with and responsible for dependent children, without a resident partner.
An arrangement in which a couple lives together without being married or in a civil partnership.
A marriage system in which an individual has more than one spouse at the same time.
A communal settlement, historically associated with Israel, in which property and child rearing are shared collectively rather than within individual family units.
